systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}
contenu:
Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Travail de recherche : utilise EXACTEMENT ces intertitres, dans cet ordre : « La question » (pourquoi ce travail, d'après l'introduction) ; « Les conclusions » (principaux résultats, avec les chiffres) ; « La méthode » (données et démarche, en quelques phrases) ; « Ce que ça implique » (explication accessible des conséquences, telles que les auteurs les présentent) ; « Les limites » (uniquement celles mentionnées par les auteurs ; omets cette section s'ils n'en mentionnent aucune). Remplis « reference » : auteurs, institution ou revue, date, et nature du document (document de travail non relu par des pairs, article de revue à comité de lecture, billet de chercheur…), uniquement d'après le texte fourni.
Source : Réserve fédérale (FEDS Notes)
Rubrique : Économie
Date du flux : 20/11/2026
Auteur : Johannes Fleck
Titre d'origine : FEDS Note: Europe’s Natural Gas Outlook for the Upcoming Winter 2026/2027

ARTICLE :
FEDS Notes
November 20, 2026
Europe’s Natural Gas Outlook for the Upcoming Winter 2026/2027
Europe is entering the 2026–27 winter with unusually low natural gas inventories. At the end of September 2026, gas storage in the EU was about 72 percent full, the lowest fill rate for that month since EU-wide data are available (from 2011) and about 11 percentage points below last September. Germany's inventories were especially low, at 58 percent full (Figure 1).2 The low inventories coincide with a tighter global market for liquefied natural gas (LNG) as the ongoing conflict in the Middle East has disrupted LNG shipments from Qatar through the Strait of Hormuz (IEA, 2026b); European wholesale gas prices have more than doubled since February.3 These developments have raised concerns about whether Europe's gas supply will last through the upcoming winter.
Against this backdrop, this note considers under what conditions Europe could face gas shortages during the 2026–27 winter. Following the analysis in Rua (2023) of Europe's energy position ahead of the 2023–24 winter, this note projects EU gas inventories through June 2027, under a Baseline and two adverse scenarios. The projections suggest that Europe can get through an average winter without running out of gas, and through a harsh winter too, albeit with stocks lower than it has tolerated in the past. However, a notable decline in LNG imports would leave storage nearly empty by the spring.
Projecting inventories requires assumptions about inflows from abroad, domestic production, and consumption, and all three now look very different from before Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The note therefore first documents how these flows have changed since 2021, using monthly data on the EU's imports by country of origin and on gas consumption, and drawing on companion work on the structural decline in gas demand.4
Inflows: Norway and LNG have replaced Russian pipeline gas
Russian gas has largely disappeared from Europe's supply. Imports from Russia fell from about 158 billion cubic meters (bcm) in 2021 to 40 bcm in 2025, or from 44 percent to 13 percent of the EU's imports from outside the EU (Figure 2).5 Since the transit contract through Ukraine expired at the end of 2024, Russian pipeline gas has reached the EU only through TurkStream (Sharples, 2025), and more than half of the remaining Russian gas arrives as LNG, which the EU has banned under short-term contracts since April 2026 and will ban under the remaining long-term contracts from January 2027.6 Norway has replaced Russia as the largest supplier of natural gas to the EU while production within the EU has fallen by 13 bcm between 2021 and 2025, mainly because the Netherlands wound down and closed the Groningen field.
LNG has filled about half of the gap left by Russian gas. LNG imports nearly doubled, from 80 bcm in 2021 to 146 bcm in 2025, when they accounted for 46 percent of imports. About three quarters of that additional LNG came from the United States. Perhaps surprisingly, despite the disruptions to global energy markets that began in February 2026, imports from outside the EU were only 1 percent lower than a year earlier during the first seven months of 2026, and LNG accounted for 45 percent of the EU's total gas imports, similar to its share for all of last year.
The reason for this resilience is that, while about one-fifth of the world's LNG passes through the Strait of Hormuz, most of it is bound for Asia and Qatar supplied only about 9 percent of the EU's LNG in 2025 and about 6 percent in the first seven months of 2026. In comparison, the United States supplied about 50 percent in 2025 and in the first seven months of 2026.7
Its new reliance on LNG makes Europe's gas supply more exposed to global market conditions. For example, as Asian buyers lose Qatari supply, they compete with Europe for cargoes from the Atlantic basin. To explore the consequences of Europe's increased exposure to the global LNG market, the Import Scarcity scenario in the analysis below focuses on the risk to the European gas supply due to LNG import reductions.
Consumption: lower, especially in winter
On the demand side, EU gas consumption fell from 413 bcm in 2021 to 332 bcm in 2024, a decline of about 20 percent (Figure 3). All end users cut back: households, industry, power plants and services. Consumption edged up slightly in 2025, mainly because power plants burned more gas. In the first seven months of 2026, Europe consumed about 1 percent more than a year earlier but still 19 percent less than during the same months of 2021.
Part of this decline reflects mild weather as heating degree days in the four winters since Russia's invasion of Ukraine were notably below normal. To isolate the decline not due to warmer winters, country-level models of monthly consumption with month effects, heating and cooling degree days and the pre-crisis level of consumption are estimated on data from January 2015 to August 2021.8 The resulting parameter estimates are used to project consumption using observed heating and cooling degree days from September 2021 onward under the relationship between heating degree days and gas consumption which existed before 2022. Thus, the gap between this weather-adjusted counterfactual and actual consumption measures the decline that is not explained by weather (Figure 4).
When accounting for weather effects in this manner, EU consumption remained about 15 percent below its pre-crisis level in 2023 to 2025. In the first seven months of 2026, the decline was about 13 percent. While the decline has narrowed somewhat in the heating season (to about 11 percent in the past two winters, from 15 percent in the two before), it has held up outside the heating season. For example, in June and July 2026, when an unusually hot summer would have raised gas use in power plants before the crisis, consumption was about a quarter below the pre-invasion counterfactual.
Inventories this winter: a baseline and two scenarios
These insights shape the projections of EU gas inventories from October 2026 through June 2027 (Figure 5), as they require basing expected consumption on the winters since the invasion. Stocks are rolled forward month by month, accounting for domestic production, net imports and consumption, starting from a stock of about 80 bcm at the end of September 2026. The first scenario ("Baseline") assumes that domestic production, imports from Russia and net imports from all other countries in each month equal their level in the same month a year earlier, and that consumption equals its average for that month over the four winters since the invasion (2022–23 to 2025–26). The second scenario ("Harsh Winter") keeps the Baseline's supply assumptions but sets consumption in each month to its maximum over those winters. Thus, even though the past four winters were relatively mild in historical comparison, this scenario still provides a meaningful representation of gas consumption under extreme weather conditions, such as the exceptionally cold winter of 2012–13, which had 14 percent more heating degree days than normal.
The third scenario ("Import Scarcity") assumes that Europe can only secure smaller LNG supplies from the global market: pipeline imports, exports and consumption are as in the Baseline, but LNG imports in each month are reduced by one-third from their level a year earlier. This is a pessimistic scenario as it assumes that Europe would have to proportionately share the decline in LNG supply due to a complete closure of the Strait of Hormuz (one-fifth of global LNG supply) and would also receive fewer deliveries from its established LNG providers, such as the United States and Algeria.9
In the Baseline scenario, inventories enter the winter well below their recent average. Storage peaks at about 84 bcm in October 2026, compared with about 99 bcm on the path implied by the 2022–25 average fill rates. Inventories fall to about 32 bcm at the end of March 2027, or 30 percent of storage capacity, before refilling begins. That is below the troughs of the past two winters but above the 20 percent of capacity to which EU countries have historically allowed stocks to fall (Rua, 2023).10
In the Harsh Winter scenario, stocks fall to about 16 bcm at the end of March 2027, or 15 percent of capacity, and stay below the 20 percent mark from February to April. In the Import Scarcity scenario, stocks fall to about 6 percent of capacity in April 2027, far below any level seen since 2011, and they remain below the 20 percent mark through June, so that refilling would start from almost zero. In all three scenarios, refilling for the 2027–28 winter would start from a lower level than this year, requiring stronger inflows than in previous years.
How much LNG could Europe lose and still get through the winter? Variants of the Import Scarcity scenario cut LNG imports to other shares of last year's level, which was about 77 bcm over October to March. With LNG at 80 percent of that level, stocks bottom out close to the Harsh Winter path. At 70 percent, they fall to about 9 bcm. At 60 percent, storage is all but empty in April 2027. In other words, a loss of about one-fifth of last year's LNG imports leaves filling levels close to the Harsh Winter path and near the critical 20 percent filling mark; beyond that, each further tenth of lost LNG imports takes roughly another 8 bcm off the trough, so that at a one-third loss storage is nearly empty and at 40 percent it is all but exhausted.
Will El Niño help?
A very strong El Niño is under way. The Oceanic Niño Index of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) reached +2.16 for July to September 2026, the highest value for that season since records began in 1950 on the traditional index, and NOAA puts the chance that the event becomes the strongest since 1950 at 83 percent for October to December.11 El Niño affects European winters mainly through the North Atlantic. According to the literature, moderate El Niño events tend to bring cold late-winter weather to northern Europe, partly because El Niño makes sudden warmings of the stratosphere, which weaken the polar vortex, more likely (Ineson and Scaife, 2009). The response reverses as events become stronger, with high pressure over the eastern Atlantic and western Europe (Toniazzo and Scaife, 2006; Ineson and others, 2026). In the five strong El Niño winters since 1980, heating degree days in the EU, weighted by gas use, were on average about 6 percent below their trend, and all five had fewer heating degree days than trend (though 1991–92 only barely).12
A winter about 6 percent milder than trend would lower non-power gas consumption by about 4 bcm in the EU. The Baseline already builds in four mild winters, however, and measured against their weather the saving shrinks to only about 2½ bcm. That cushion is also uncertain because the evidence rests on only five winters, the event expected this year would be stronger than any of them, and the stratospheric channel that brings late-winter cold spells cannot be ruled out: no sudden stratospheric warming occurred in the strong El Niño winters of 1982–83, 1997–98 and 2015–16, but one did in 1972–73 and another in January 2024, with little effect on the surface (Ineson and others, 2026). Thus, a very strong El Niño improves the odds for Europe's gas balances to last through the upcoming winter, but it does not rule out the cold snaps that matter most when storage is low.
